Moxibustion burns mugwort (Artemisia) near points. Cupping uses vacuum, electroacupuncture uses a weak current, and auricular acupuncture works on the ear.

Moxibustion uses Artemisia (mugwort) leaves burned near points. Traditionally, it is said to "warm the meridians" and expel "cold". Types: direct moxibustion (a small cone on the skin, which can leave a scar and is rarely practiced), indirect moxibustion (with a layer of ginger, garlic or salt between the cone and the skin), the moxa stick held above the skin, and box moxibustion. The main risk is burns, followed by smoke, which can irritate the airways; the space must be ventilated. Avoid it in case of fever, on damaged skin, on the face, in pregnancy (abdominal area) and in people with reduced sensation. Evidence: there are studies for some situations, such as turning a fetus from breech presentation, but quality is variable and it does not replace obstetric care.

Not all points are equal in the tradition. Some have special roles, and knowing them helps in reading protocols. The Yuan (source) points are considered places where the organ's original Qi concentrates; on the yin meridians they usually coincide with the Shu point (for example LU9, HT7, KI3), while on the yang meridians they are separate (LI4, ST42, GB40). The Luo (connecting) points bridge the yin meridian and its coupled yang meridian; examples: LU7, PC6, ST40.

Not everything related to points is equally well founded. Classical acupuncture has studies, with mixed results; other practices look scientific but lack evidence. Recognizing the difference is a skill.

For primary dysmenorrhea, acupressure at SP6 and acupuncture have moderate-level evidence from meta-analyses (variable quality) regarding pain reduction; the results should be interpreted with caution.
For TMJ pain acupuncture has limited evidence; massage and relaxation can help, but dental treatment remains the basis.
For neck pain, acupuncture and massage have limited to moderate evidence of short-term relief; acupressure mainly brings muscle relaxation and comfort.
For shoulder pain there is limited evidence that acupuncture helps in the short term; acupressure remains a comfort adjunct, not a treatment for the injury.
For postoperative dental pain acupuncture has limited evidence; acupressure may offer only a temporary comfort effect and does not treat the cause.
For musculoskeletal pain there are weak signals, but many studies are of low quality.
For fibromyalgia, acupuncture and gentle movement (tai chi, qigong) have low- to moderate-level evidence regarding pain and sleep; acupressure is mainly a relaxation adjunct.
For nausea in pregnancy, Cochrane reviews show low- to moderate-level evidence that stimulating PC6 may help some women; the results are inconsistent and the effect is modest.

For postoperative nausea, stimulation of PC6 (including acupressure) has low-quality evidence versus sham and moderate-quality evidence of equivalence with antiemetics (Cochrane 2015); for chemotherapy-related nausea a 2023 meta-analysis shows benefits, but the studies are few and heterogeneous; evidence is limited for fatigue, anxiety and pain.

For insomnia, acupuncture has low- to moderate-level evidence regarding sleep quality; for acupressure small studies show modest improvements, with a risk of bias. CBT-I remains the first-line treatment.

For chronic low back pain, acupuncture (with needles) has moderate-level evidence for short-term pain reduction, with part of the effect being nonspecific. For acupressure alone the evidence is weaker; it may bring relaxation and comfort alongside movement and exercise.
For nonspecific fatigue the evidence is limited; some studies show short-lived improvements with acupressure (for example in chronically ill patients), but the quality is modest.
For the eyes, press only on the bone around the orbit, never on the eyeball.

For migraine prophylaxis, acupuncture has moderate-level evidence (Cochrane reviews) for reducing attack frequency, comparable in some studies to preventive medication; for acupressure the evidence is limited.
For allergic rhinitis, acupuncture (with needles) has moderate evidence of symptom relief in small studies; for acupressure the evidence is limited.
For mild to moderate symptoms, acupuncture and laser acupuncture have limited evidence regarding pain relief; acupressure alone has no solid evidence, but may be an adjunct to a splint.
For tinnitus, acupuncture has weak and inconsistent evidence; guidelines do not recommend it routinely. Acupressure may possibly help through relaxation.
For chronic urticaria, acupuncture has limited evidence from small studies; acupressure has no solid evidence and does not replace antihistamines.
For overactive bladder, tibial stimulation (TENS/acupuncture) has moderate-level evidence for reducing urgency; for acupressure alone the evidence is limited.

A placebo is a treatment without an active mechanism, which can nevertheless improve symptoms through expectation, attention and context. In acupuncture, "sham" (simulation) is used: needles that do not penetrate (Streitberger retractable needles) or needling at "wrong" points. The problem: sham acupuncture can also stimulate the skin, so it may have an effect of its own. If the difference between real acupuncture and sham is small, there are two interpretations: either the exact point does not matter much, or it does, but the sham is not inert. That is why several types of comparison are useful: acupuncture vs. sham, vs. no treatment and vs. standard treatment.
Placebo can reduce symptoms (especially pain), so trials need a control group.
